                                    COMMENTS OF VISTRA CORP.

            Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”), October 27,

     2025, notice in the above-captioned proceeding, Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby respectfully

     submits these comments on the Secretary of Energy’s letter regarding the interconnection of large

     loads and the accompanying Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposal (“DOE ANOPR

     Proposal”).

I.      INTRODUCTION

            The proposal in Secretary Wright’s letter is an idea whose time has come. And not a

     moment too soon. The world is facing a historic inflection point as artificial intelligence (“AI”),

     machine learning, and other advanced computing applications are poised to transform the

     economic landscape and shape the future of the global economy. In much the same way that the

     proliferation of steam engines drove the industrial revolution, data centers and other digital

     infrastructure will drive this next transformational period. But data centers require electricity, and

     our ability to develop the infrastructure needed to lead the world is being hindered by slow-moving

     and unsettled regulatory processes that stymie the deployment of the necessary digital

     infrastructure. Secretary Wright’s letter provides the roadmap the nation needs to break that
 logjam and unlock that digital infrastructure to ensure that the United States’s computing prowess

remains world leading.

        That is why Secretary Wright is entirely correct that the “timely, orderly, and non-

discriminatory” interconnection of large loads, including data centers, to the transmission system

is critical to ensuring American prosperity as well as the affordability, reliability, and security of

our electric system.1      Access to power is becoming the limiting element for data center

development. The national security implications of his proposal are equally stark given that, as he

has previously observed, the development of AI capabilities supported by data centers and other

digital infrastructure represents a national security imperative that is nothing less than the “next

Manhattan project.”2 Those conclusions flow inexorably from the President’s observation this

past summer that we are competing with China and other nations in a “race to achieve global

dominance in artificial intelligence,” with the winner securing the ability to “set global AI

standards and reap broad economic and military benefits.”3 This proceeding has the potential to

help win that race.

         Secretary Wright is similarly correct that “the interconnection of large loads directly to the

interstate transmission system to access the transmission system and the electricity transmitted

over it falls squarely within the Commission's jurisdiction.”4 His conclusion is consistent with the

           Vistra applauds Secretary Wright for his action in initiating this proceeding. In the balance

  of these comments, Vistra explains why Secretary Wright’s theory of jurisdiction is correct, why

  it is critical for the Commission to exercise that jurisdiction now, how the Commission should

  approach the transition to any new reforms it adopts, and how the Commission should approach

  certain threshold questions implicated by the DOE ANOPR Proposal.

II.   JURISDICTION

           As Secretary Wright’s proposal makes clear, in promulgating rules for large load

  interconnection, the “Commission’s jurisdiction should be limited to interconnection directly to

 transmission facilities, consistent with the Commission’s seven-factor test.”12 It is critical to

address at the outset the extent to which this jurisdictional theory is indeed “limited” and properly

respects the scope of state authority. States exercise significant authority to regulate crucial aspects

of large loads, such as the terms and conditions of retail sales to large loads,13 siting new generation

facilities to serve large loads, and load interconnections to the distribution system.14                              This

proceeding will not shrink any of those critical functions, which are properly regulated at the state

level. Rather, the Commission, for its part, would only regulate the interconnection to the

transmission system, which falls within the plenary transmission jurisdiction that the FPA reserves

for the Commission. Given the regulatory uncertainty that has crippled the industry for the last 18

months, a clear statement from the Commission to unequivocally exert jurisdiction over

transmission-level load interconnections will provide needed certainty to the markets and states.

This task is all the more pressing given that there is no doubt as to where jurisdiction over

transmission-level load interconnection lies.

         The interconnection of retail loads to the transmission system is within the Commission’s

exclusive jurisdiction under sections 201, 205, and 206 of the FPA.15 Those provisions vest the

Commission with jurisdiction over wholesale sales of electricity in interstate commerce and the

transmission of electricity in interstate commerce.16 That jurisdiction extends to “[a]ll rates and

         The Commission’s jurisdiction over the transmission of electricity in interstate commerce

is broader than its jurisdiction with respect to wholesale sales of electricity.18 Congress gave the

Commission “jurisdiction over all facilities for [the] transmission or sale of electric energy” with

the exception of “facilities used for the generation of electric energy or over facilities used in local

distribution or only for the transmission of electric energy in intrastate commerce, or over facilities

for the transmission of electric energy consumed wholly by the transmitter.”19 By contrast,

Congress expressly reserved to the states jurisdiction “over facilities used for the generation of

electric energy.”20 Accordingly, the Commission’s jurisdiction with respect to the transmission of

electricity extends to the rates, charges, and practices affecting such sales and the transmission

facilities themselves, whereas with respect to the wholesale sale of electricity, the Commission’s

jurisdiction extends to rates, charges, and practices affecting such sales but not to the generation

facilities themselves. As the U.S. Supreme Court has observed, the FPA limits the Commission’s

jurisdiction over sales of electricity to wholesale sales (i.e., sales for resale), but it does not limit

the Commission’s jurisdiction over the transmission of electricity to the transmission necessary to

over transmission rates and transmission facilities themselves. Interconnection procedures for

both loads and generators determine how those interconnection facilities and network upgrades

are identified, developed, paid for, and used. If the Commission does not regulate interconnection

         Finally, a contrary conclusion would produce exactly the sort of regulatory gap that the

Supreme Court in EPSA concluded does not exist under the FPA.33 Transmission-level load

interconnection cannot fall within the states’ ambit. If it did, loads that interconnect to the

transmission system would do so under state-jurisdictional tariffs and state public utility

commissions would be left to determine, for example, how transmission-level interconnection

facilities and network upgrades are studied, selected, and funded. That would plainly infringe

upon the Commission’s plenary transmission jurisdiction.34 And given this ineluctable fact,

transmission-level load interconnection must be within the Commission’s jurisdiction, otherwise

it would fall into a “limbo area[] unregulated by federal or state authorities.”35

transmission rates, which provides the Commission with an independent rationale to exert

         Large load interconnection procedures easily satisfy both prongs of the EPSA two-step

inquiry.37 First, just as in EPSA where the demand response rules, particularly the formula for

compensating demand response,38 would necessarily and directly affect wholesale electricity

procedures affect transmission facilities, which are themselves within the Commission’s authority

to regulate, the Commission has an additional jurisdictional hook here that was not available in

EPSA. As such, transmission-level load interconnections present an even more compelling case

for Commission jurisdiction than the wholesale demand response rules in EPSA.

          As to the second prong of the EPSA analysis, while the procedures governing transmission-

level load interconnection might have a significant, albeit indirect, effect on retail sales, that “is of

no legal consequence” to the jurisdictional analysis. That is because the FPA does not create

“hermetically sealed” spheres of state and federal jurisdiction.39 Rather, the rates and other actions

within the Commission’s sphere of exclusive jurisdiction have “natural consequences” within the

states’ sphere of jurisdiction.40 “And so too, of necessity, will FERC’s regulation of those

wholesale matters.”41

         Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo does not affect the jurisdictional analysis under

either EPSA or New York v. FERC.42 EPSA explicitly disclaimed reliance on Chevron deference,

stating that FERC’s authority is “clear.”43 In New York v. FERC, the Court described the FPA’s

broad grant of authority over transmission jurisdiction as “clear statutory language,” and Chevron

was relevant only to the Court’s narrower review of the Commission’s policy decision to refrain

from exerting jurisdiction over a particular type of transaction.44 Accordingly, if anything, it is the

Commission’s decision in Order No. 888 not to assert a broader theory of jurisdiction that is

rendered vulnerable by Loper Bright.

III.   NEED FOR REFORM

           Winning the global AI race will require enormous investments in digital infrastructure,

   particularly data centers, and the associated energy infrastructure to supply the necessary

   electricity. But those investments will be made in the United States if, and only if, the relevant

   regulatory regime provides the predictability, stability, and durability needed to facilitate such

   significant outlays of private capital. To date, regulatory uncertainty is at its zenith because the

   Commission has not acted in its most significant proceedings involving data center development

   and the one order it did issue raised more questions than it provided answers.66 This proceeding—

   and other pending dockets—provide a chance to fill that regulatory vacuum by replacing opaque

   or non-existent rules governing transmission-level interconnection procedures with a regulatory

   regime sufficient to meet the moment. In so doing, the Commission can augment positive

 Study Agreement as of the effective date of the Final Rule, the Interconnection Customer will have the option to either
 continue with the rest of its Interconnection Studies under the Transmission Provider's existing study process or
 complete those remaining studies for which it does not have a signed Interconnection Study Agreement under the
 Final Rule LGIP.”)
     87
        Id. P 187.

                                                          27
           A. Any New Interconnection Procedures Must Apply Specifically to Interconnections
             to the Transmission System

          The Commission must structure its reforms in a manner that is consistent with the

jurisdictional lines established in the FPA. As explained above, the Commission’s authority to act

in this arena is based on its jurisdiction over the transmission system. That statutory authority

controls how any large load interconnection procedures could be structured.

          The DOE ANOPR Proposal correctly identified this dynamic in explaining that the

Commission’s load interconnection reforms should only apply where the load will interconnect

directly to transmission facilities, consistent with the Commission’s seven-factor test.88 Although

the Commission’s pro forma generator interconnection procedures apply, in certain instances, to

interconnections to distribution facilities—such as where a distribution facility is “used to transmit

electric energy in interstate commerce on behalf of a wholesale purchaser pursuant to a

Commission-filed OATT”89—the Commission cannot follow that approach here. New large loads,

unlike wholesale generators, typically do not engage in wholesale power transactions. The

Commission’s jurisdiction is based solely on the physical interconnection to a Commission-

jurisdictional transmission facility.

          For a similar reason, FERC should not adopt the 20 MW threshold proposed in the DOE

ANOPR Proposal. The 20 MW threshold does not appear to be tied to any particular conclusion

about the interaction between the large load and the transmission system. Rather, the Commission

should consider a MW threshold at a level that corresponds to likely use of or impact on the

transmission system.


—————————————————
   88
        DOE ANOPR Proposal at P 18.
   89
        Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103 at P 804.

                                                      28
           B. Interconnection Studies Must be Structured to Address Transmission System
             Upgrades and Cannot be Used To Address Resource Adequacy Concerns

          Relatedly, and in keeping with these principles, the studies involving the interconnection

of new loads must focus on studying the impacts to the transmission system. As noted above,

states retain jurisdiction over generation facilities.90 With that in mind, and consistent with the

Commission’s jurisdiction over the transmission system—and interconnections to it—load

interconnection studies must be focused on identifying the transmission system upgrades needed

to facilitate the interconnection and allocating the costs of those upgrades in a manner consistent

with the Commission’s cost causation principles.

          This approach is consistent with the Commission’s treatment of all other analogous studies,

including generator interconnection studies and generator deactivation studies. Interconnection

processes have always been focused on the transmission facilities needed to accommodate

interconnection service, while markets remain focused on aligning supply and demand. To do

otherwise risks producing ill-conceived, and perhaps unlawful, policies that undermine the

efficacy of the Commission’s various regulatory frameworks. This principle must apply to both

standalone load and to loads co-located with generating facilities, including instances in which a

new load seeks to co-locate with an existing generator. An existing generating facility serving a

new co-located load has the same impact on resource adequacy as the addition of a new standalone

load of the same size. Moreover, to treat these loads differently would ignore the fact that, as the

D.C. Circuit has explained, every user of the transmission system is economically marginal,

meaning that increased demand on a system can be attributed to every load, regardless of whether



—————————————————
   90
        Supra note 20.

                                                  29
 they are existing or incremental, co-located or standalone.91                   It would therefore be unduly

discriminatory to apply a resource adequacy study only for the addition of behind-the-meter co-

located load and not to a new standalone load.92 And, as noted above, the Commission cannot

impose such a study in new load interconnection procedures without crossing important

jurisdictional boundaries.

         Using the load interconnection process to address resource adequacy issues would also

place resource adequacy obligations on the wrong entity. New loads coming onto the system only

create a resource adequacy issue if an LSE signs up new customers without sufficient generation

resources to serve those loads. LSEs should be responsible for resolving resource adequacy issues

that they have allowed to arise. Otherwise, the burden will be doled out piecemeal to new load

seeking to interconnect to the grid, which will further slow the pace of infrastructure and data

center development.

         The consideration of resource adequacy issues in load interconnection studies may also

grant LSEs a new ability to exercise undue discrimination. LSEs often have nearly unbounded

discretion in producing load forecasts,93 which is one of the primary tools used to assess whether

a resource adequacy concern might arise. Unlike transmission system impacts, which can be




—————————————————
    91
        See BNP Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d 264, 268 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (citation omitted).
    92
        See, e.g., Transmission Agency of N. Cal. v. FERC, 628 F.3d 538, 551 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (explaining that the
Commission cannot treat similarly situated entities differently (citing Sacramento Mun. Util. Dist. v. FERC, 474 F.3d
797, 802 (D.C. Cir. 2007))); N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 162 FERC ¶ 61,124, at P 10 (2018) (“To say that entities
are similarly situated does not mean that there are no differences between them; rather, it means that there are no
differences that are material to the inquiry at hand.”).
     93
        In PJM, for instance, LSEs are allowed to use any methodology of their choice in proposing adjustments to the
load forecast to account for expected large loads. PJM, Manual 19: Load Forecasting and Analysis, Revision 37,
attach. B (Dec. 18, 2024), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m19.pdf. There are no binding
guidelines on the methodology that LSEs use or how PJM incorporates those inputs into its load forecast.

                                                         30
 modeled and measured by independent consultants, resource adequacy projections involve a much

greater level of subjectivity, which LSEs could use to preference certain projects over others.

         While it is inappropriate to include resource adequacy in load interconnection studies for

the reasons described above, there are a number of other actions the Commission can and should

take to protect resource adequacy. For instance, as the DOE ANOPR Proposal suggested, the

Commission could incentivize loads to agree to be curtailable through expedited interconnection

access.94 The Commission can also support load forecasting reforms to better understand the true

extent of resource adequacy needs, as well as capacity market reforms to ensure that Commission-

jurisdictional capacity markets send accurate price signals. The Commission has many tools in its

toolbox to protect resource adequacy. It need not—and cannot—resort to measures that cross

jurisdictional boundaries, introduce new sources of possible undue discrimination, and cast doubt

on the legal durability of the rules that the Commission adopts in this proceeding.

         C. The Commission Should Facilitate the Co-Location of Load and Generation at the
            Same Point of Interconnection

         The DOE ANOPR Proposal recognizes that developing load and generation in close

proximity can expedite study processes and minimize the need for costly network upgrades.95 As

noted above, the co-location of load and generation at a single point of interconnection—represents

the lowest hanging fruit for the Commission to make significant progress quickly in facilitating

the infrastructure needed to win the AI race.

         In the near term, the Commission can facilitate co-location arrangements involving an

existing generator without creating new study procedures. For instance, PJM’s necessary study


—————————————————
   94
        DOE ANOPR Proposal at P 24.
   95
        See id. P 20.

                                                31
 process already can be used to add behind-the-meter co-located load to existing generation

facilities. Under this framework, PJM studies the arrangement to determine whether it requires

changes to the interconnection facilities or triggers a need for new transmission network upgrades.

The generator bears the costs of any such interconnection facilities and network upgrades,96 thus

ensuring that other customers do not bear the cost of network upgrades needed to accommodate

new behind-the-meter co-located load. That framework is the fastest way to make progress in

building the digital infrastructure needed to meet the moment because both the rules and the points

of interconnection already exist.

         To contrast, co-location arrangements involving new generators will require new tariff

language to effectuate the coordinated and expedited study of new load co-located with new

generation. The Commission should prioritize doing so as soon as possible because it “will allow

for efficient siting of loads and generating facilities and thereby minimize the need for costly

network upgrades.”97 It is also the most promising reform that the Commission could adopt

expeditiously because it can most readily draw on the Commission’s experience regulating

generator interconnections. In the course of this proceeding, the Commission could consider

whether those new rules should—on a prospective basis—replace existing generator modification

processes that govern the co-location of new loads with existing resources.              In either

arrangement—whether the co-location configuration involves a new or existing generator—the

Commission should apply the common-sense principles from the DOE ANOPR that promote the

most efficient use of the transmission system and ensure just and reasonable rates. First, the



—————————————————
   96
        See DOE ANOPR Proposal at P 25.
   97
        Id. P 20.

                                                32
       facilities should be studied based on their withdrawal or injection rights.98 Accurately reflecting

      the proposed behavior of a facility ensures the reliable interconnection of these facilities without

      overestimating their impact on the transmission system.99 Second, in keeping with the cost

      causation principle, transmission service charges should be based on actual use of the transmission

      system, as measured by the facility’s net load.100

VI.       CONCLUSION

               The Commission must heed Secretary Wright’s call to action and use this proceeding—

      and this moment—to provide regulatory certainty and clear rules to govern how large loads

      interconnect to the interstate transmission system. Doing so is critical for national security,

      national prosperity, and the fulfillment of the Commission’s responsibilities under the Federal

      Power Act. We urge the Commission to follow the roadmap provided above to unlock investment

      in the infrastructure needed to power the AI revolution.               The Commission can and must

      immediately alleviate regulatory uncertainty and create durable rules that will govern the next

      generation of investments in the nation’s electrical and digital infrastructure.

Definitions

For purposes of this schedule:

“Contract” means the service agreement entered into by the customer and the Company in accordance with this
schedule.

“Contract Capacity” means the mutually agreed amount of monthly peak load requirements for each month during
the remaining term after the Load Ramp Period as set forth in the contract for service, whereby the Company agrees

CRES provider supply of generation service) subject to the terms and conditions in its tariffs and the customer agrees
to purchase service at that level for the stated term of the contract under the same terms and conditions.”

“Data Center” means a centralized facility (a) used primarily or exclusively for electronic information services such
as the management, storage, processing, and dissemination of electronic data and information through the use of
computer systems, servers, networking equipment, and related components that (b) has an aggregate monthly
maximum demand of greater than 25,000 kW. Unless otherwise specified, the term “Data Center” shall include
“Mobile Data Center.”

“Mobile Data Center” means a centralized facility (a) used primarily or exclusively for electronic information services
such as the management, storage, processing, and dissemination of electronic data and information (including
mining of cryptocurrency) through the use of computer systems, servers, networking equipment, and related
components that (b) has an aggregate monthly maximum demand of greater than 25,000 kW and has load that is
portable and/or distributable, including but not limited to structures that are not affixed to the ground or are easily
removed from a location.

“Single Location” refers to an area that is owned, operated, or leased by the Data Center customer with the metering
point for the customer’s metering point. A contiguous lot (or lots) to the area with the customer’s metering point
may be considered the customer’s premises regardless of easements, public thoroughfares, transportation rights-
of-way, or utility rights-of-way, so long as it would not create an unsafe or hazardous condition.

“Load Ramp Contract Capacity” means the mutually agreed monthly peak load requirements associated with the
Load Ramp Period. The Load Ramp Contract Capacity shall not be less than:

           In Year 1, 50% of Contract Capacity.
           In Year 2, 65% of Contract Capacity.
           In Year 3, 80% of Contract Capacity.
           In Year 4, 90% of Contract Capacity.

“Load Ramp Period” refers to the time of commencement of service until the customer reaches full contract capacity,
which shall not exceed four years.

“Existing Load” means Data Center load for which a letter of agreement or electric service agreement has already
been signed by the effective date of Schedule DCT.

Customers qualifying for this schedule that execute an electric service agreement with the Company or expand their
current contracted capacity after the effective date of this tariff are required to take service under this schedule and

Schedule DCT does not apply to Existing Load above 25,000 kW that has already signed a letter of agreement or
electric service agreement by the effective date of Schedule DCT, so long as the Existing Load does not expand by
more than 25,000 kW above the contracted capacity under the existing electric service agreement following the
effective date of Schedule DCT. Schedule DCT will apply to an Existing Load that signs a new electric service

incurred by AEP Ohio to complete such separate metering. If the load is not separately metered, then the Existing
Load will lose its Existing Load status and become subject to Schedule DCT.

If the customer facility operates one or more Data Centers with a monthly maximum demand of greater than 25,000
kW and has non-Data Center load (that would otherwise be billed under the General Service or other applicable
